clue.text: They're not used by stonewallers in cricket

definitions.text: They're not used by stonewallers in cricket

parts.words: They're not used by stonewallers in cricket
parts.note: a stonewaller in cricket is a dogged defensive batsman, but read as a builder of stone walls he uses stone, not fired clay, so the bats here are brick ones

explanation.surface: A remark about the sort of bat that defensive batsmen never pick up.
explanation.walkthrough: A stonewaller in cricket is a batsman who just blocks the ball. Read as someone building in stone, he would not use bricks, and the 'bats' are pieces of brick: brickbats are lumps of brick thrown as missiles.
explanation.definitionFit: Brickbats are broken pieces of brick, the kind of rubble thrown as missiles, which a builder in stone would never handle.

clue.text: If he made a breach, his son would not in a wine-cask

definitions.text: his son would not in a wine-cask

indicators.note: 'If he made a breach' means if this man were made into the word breach by rearrangement

explanation.surface: A riddle about a man breaking through, and his son avoiding the wine barrel.
explanation.walkthrough: In Jeremiah 35 the sons of Rechab refuse wine, so his son would not be found in a wine-cask; rearranging the name gives BREACH.
explanation.definitionFit: Rechab's descendant Jonadab ordered his family to drink no wine, so the biblical father's son stayed out of the wine-cask.

clue.text: A short account would put this benefice absolutely right

indicators.note: the clue says that putting the short account before this word would make the word for absolutely right, so take it away again

parts.note: complete correctness is accuracy
A/C is the short form of account

explanation.surface: Claiming a brief bookkeeping entry would fix a church living.
explanation.walkthrough: 'would put' reads as an addition: the short account placed in front of the answer would give the word for absolutely right, so the solver takes it away again.
explanation.definitionFit: A curate's post, the office held under a vicar or rector, is a church benefice.

clue.text: Church built of quartz to some degree

indicators.note: 'to' says the degree is joined to the word for quartz

parts.note: BA is a Bachelor of Arts, a university degree
quartz is a form of silica, silicon dioxide

explanation.surface: A church whose walls are partly made of quartz.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to some degree' looks like 'partly'; it is BA, a degree, joined onto SILICA.
explanation.definitionFit: A basilica is a large oblong church, in the Roman Catholic Church one granted special status.

clue.text: Support for a settler, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps says the letters of settler might be put some other way

explanation.surface: A suggestion about how a pioneer might be helped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges SETTLER; the surface makes 'support for a settler' backing for a pioneer.
explanation.definitionFit: A trestle is a frame of a beam on two pairs of legs used to hold up a table top.

clue.text: Here even the most wary may be caught on the hop

definitions.text: Here even the most wary may be caught on the hop

parts.words: Here even the most wary may be caught on the hop
parts.note: to be caught on the hop is to be taken unawares, but a hop is also a dance, so here everyone is dancing

explanation.surface: A place where even careful people are taken by surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caught on the hop' means surprised; a hop is an informal dance, and anyone at one is literally on the hop.
explanation.definitionFit: A large room for dancing is where people at a hop are found.

clue.text: Where more than half of 1 are made to measure ?

definitions.text: Where more than half of 1 are made to measure ?

parts.words: Where more than half of 1 are made to measure ?
parts.note: the first five of the nine letters of 1 across name the things made, and 'measure' is a unit of length

explanation.surface: Asking where goods are tailored to order.
explanation.walkthrough: 1 across is BRICKBATS; more than half of it is BRICK(S), which are made here, and a yard is a measure. 'Made to measure' suggests tailoring.
explanation.definitionFit: A brickworks is a place where bricks are made, and the place name's second half is also a unit of length.

clue.text: She daren't upset her followers

indicators.note: upset means the letters of the first two words are knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: A woman too nervous to upset her supporters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' looks like the verb she daren't do; it rearranges SHE DARENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Supporters of a cause or leader are those who stick to it.

clue.text: "Where Alph, the river ran " (Coleridge)

parts.note: a quotation from the poem Kubla Khan with one word missing; the gap before 'river' is what the solver supplies

explanation.surface: A fill-in-the-blank quotation from Coleridge's poem Kubla Khan.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed clue has a dash before 'river' marking the gap. The line in Kubla Khan runs 'Where Alph, the sacred river, ran', so the missing word is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Coleridge's Kubla Khan describes the river Alph as holy, and that adjective is the word missing from the quoted line.

clue.text: A hundred locks — for stage doors, of course !

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
locks of hair are tresses

explanation.surface: A remark about a hundred locks fitted to the doors of a theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Locks' and 'stage doors' suggest a theatre's security, but locks are hair and 'stage doors' is read as people who do the stage, performers.
explanation.definitionFit: Women who perform on the stage are its 'doers', the players found at any theatre's stage door.

clue.text: Hat for garden use ?

definitions.meaning: a close-fitting bell-shaped women's hat of the 1920s
a glass or plastic cover put over young plants in a garden

explanation.surface: A hat that seems to be meant for wearing while gardening.
explanation.definitionFit: The word, French for bell, names both a bell-shaped hat and a bell-shaped protective cover for seedlings.

clue.text: Suitable name for a busy surgeon ?

definitions.text: Suitable name for a busy surgeon ?

parts.words: Suitable name for a busy surgeon ?
parts.note: a surgeon cuts with a lancet, so a busy one would lance a lot; the name of a knight of the Round Table sounds just like that

explanation.surface: A suggestion for what to call a hard-working surgeon.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the name of King Arthur's knight into LANCE and LOT: a busy surgeon lances a lot.
explanation.definitionFit: The Arthurian knight's name breaks into two words describing a surgeon who cuts open boils and abscesses very often.

clue.text: Floor-covering pattern in the printing room

parts.note: lino is short for linoleum, a floor covering
a type is a pattern or model

explanation.surface: A floor covering of some pattern found in a print works.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the lino on the print room floor; in fact the two pieces join to name a typesetting machine.
explanation.definitionFit: A Linotype was the hot-metal typesetting machine that stood in every newspaper composing room.

clue.text: For the card-sharper, the punishment seems to fit the crime

definitions.text: For the card-sharper, the punishment seems to fit the crime

parts.words: For the card-sharper, the punishment seems to fit the crime
parts.note: a military punishment of marching with full kit has a name that also describes a cheat's practised handling of a deck of cards

explanation.surface: A remark that a cheat at cards got the punishment he deserved.
explanation.walkthrough: Pack drill was a soldier's punishment of drilling in full pack; for a cheat it also describes drilling a pack of cards.
explanation.definitionFit: The old army punishment of marching in full kit has a name that reads as practising with a deck of cards.

clue.text: One of the peculiarities of men in arms

definitions.text: One of the peculiarities of men in arms

indicators.note: a peculiar version of the words that follow is a strange arrangement of their letters

explanation.surface: Describing a habit typical of soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'peculiarities of' signals that the letters of MEN IN ARMS are rearranged; the whole clue also says what the result is, a soldier's habit.
explanation.definitionFit: A habitual gesture or way of speaking that marks a person out is a peculiarity of behaviour.

clue.text: What does Father make of the R.A.F. ?

definitions.text: What does Father make of the R.A.F. ?

parts.words: What does Father make of the R.A.F. ?
parts.note: read as letters, 'the RAF' rearranged makes the word father; the question asks what one word is of the other

explanation.surface: Asking what Dad thinks of the Royal Air Force.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of THE RAF can be rearranged to spell FATHER, so FATHER is a rearrangement of THE RAF, and the clue asks the name for that relation.
explanation.definitionFit: A word made by rearranging the letters of another is the term asked for, and father and 'the RAF' share all six letters.

clue.text: Estate agents reach true heights in America

parts.note: true means real
tors are rocky hills or peaks

explanation.surface: Property dealers reaching new heights across the Atlantic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in America' says the answer is the American word; a TOR is a rocky hill, common on Dartmoor in Devon.
explanation.definitionFit: In the US a property broker who sells houses and land carries this title.

clue.text: It's a fault for me returning extremely fatigued

indicators.note: extremely says the word for fatigued sits at the extremes, either side of me
returning means the whole assembly is read backwards

parts.note: fatigued means tired
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone owning up that it was their fault for coming back worn out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremely' sets the word for fatigued at either side of 'me', and 'returning' turns the result round. The surface makes 'extremely fatigued' one phrase meaning exhausted.
explanation.definitionFit: A demerit is a black mark recorded against someone for a failing or offence.

clue.text: What the soldier said was not this, Sam Weller was told

definitions.text: What the soldier said was not this, Sam Weller was told

parts.words: What the soldier said was not this, Sam Weller was told
parts.note: in Dickens's Pickwick Papers the judge rules that what the soldier said cannot be admitted in court

explanation.surface: A line recalling a courtroom scene from Dickens.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Pickwick Papers Sam Weller, giving testimony, is rebuked by the judge: 'You must not tell us what the soldier, or any other man, said, sir; it's not evidence.'
explanation.definitionFit: Hearsay of a soldier's words was ruled inadmissible as proof in court in Dickens's novel.

clue.text: This person is certainly not particular

definitions.text: This person is certainly not particular

parts.words: This person is certainly not particular
parts.note: particular usually means fussy, but here it means specific: a person left unnamed

explanation.surface: Describing a person who is not fussy at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not particular' suggests easy-going; it means not a specific individual, an unspecified person.
explanation.definitionFit: An unidentified individual, not any particular one, is meant by this indefinite pronoun.

clue.text: Jumper fitted with a pocket, naturally

definitions.text: Jumper fitted with a pocket, naturally

parts.words: Jumper fitted with a pocket, naturally
parts.note: a jumper is a sweater, but also an animal that jumps; this jumper's pocket is a pouch it is born with

explanation.surface: Describing a sweater that comes with a pocket.
explanation.walkthrough: In British English a jumper is a sweater; here it is an animal that jumps, and its pocket is the marsupial pouch it grows naturally.
explanation.definitionFit: The Australian marsupial travels by hopping and the female carries her young in a pouch.

clue.text: Song and dance to a copper

parts.note: a ball is a formal dance
D stood for the old penny, a copper coin

explanation.surface: A song-and-dance act performed for a policeman.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'copper' is slang for a policeman but here is a copper coin, the old British penny, abbreviated D.
explanation.definitionFit: A ballad is a narrative song or a simple sentimental one.

clue.text: The relative who helps us to be in the money

indicators.note: the clue says this relative helps us to be in the money, putting us inside the word for money

parts.note: coin is money
taken as written

explanation.surface: A relative who helps the family get rich.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be in the money' is an idiom for being rich; read literally, the word 'us' sits inside a word for money.
explanation.definitionFit: The child of one's aunt or uncle is a family relation.

clue.text: The central figure in a dispute, perhaps

definitions.text: The central figure in a dispute, perhaps

parts.words: The central figure in a dispute, perhaps
parts.note: the person standing in the middle of a quarrel is not one of the sides but the go-between

explanation.surface: Asking who stands at the heart of a quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: The obvious reading is the main party to a quarrel; the clue means the person literally in the middle, between the two sides.
explanation.definitionFit: A go-between who negotiates between two quarrelling sides sits in the middle of the dispute.

clue.text: It's scarcely noticeable

parts.note: read as 'it is noticeable for being scarce': something seen because it is so seldom found

explanation.surface: Describing something so faint it can hardly be seen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scarcely noticeable' normally means hard to see; read it as noticeable because scarce, which is what makes a collector's item stand out.
explanation.definitionFit: Something uncommon is remarkable precisely because it is scarce.

clue.text: Unrestricted state of an incapacitated 21 ?

definitions.meaning: the jumping animal at 21 across moves by hops, so one unable to do so would be lacking its leaps

explanation.surface: Asking how to describe a jumping animal that can no longer move freely.
explanation.walkthrough: 21 across is the Australian marsupial that moves in bounds; one that could not leap would be without bounds.
explanation.definitionFit: Having no limits is being without bounds, and a lamed hopping animal would equally be without its leaps.

clue.text: They keep to the beaten track

definitions.text: They keep to the beaten track

parts.words: They keep to the beaten track
parts.note: a beaten track is a well-worn path, but read literally it is the track of those who are beaten in a contest

explanation.surface: Describing cautious walkers who never stray from familiar paths.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The beaten track' is the familiar route; here 'beaten' means defeated, so those who keep to it are the ones who always come off worst.
explanation.definitionFit: People who are always defeated stay on the path of the beaten.

clue.text: One who doesn't have to be enjoined to " hang on "

definitions.text: One who doesn't have to be enjoined to " hang on "

parts.words: One who doesn't have to be enjoined to " hang on "
parts.note: to hang on someone is to rely on them for support, so a person who relies on another needs no order to do so

explanation.surface: Someone who needs no telling to wait.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hang on' looks like 'wait'; it means rely on, so the person meant leans on another for support without being told.
explanation.definitionFit: A person relying on another for financial support is that person's charge, for instance a child or spouse.
